title: How to structure a training session
summary: A plan for one session: a short warm-up, one or two kinds of target, doubles after singles and a finish on targets that go well.

body.html: A session with a plan usually does more than shooting whatever is on offer. Without a plan you tire sooner and repeat the same faults. With a coach the plan is usually theirs, but it helps to know what a session is made of.

Start with a warm-up: light movement for the neck, shoulders, back and wrists, then a few easy targets to find your rhythm. This way the movement is more likely to be smooth from the first target. How to do it: Warm-up and mobility.

The main part is usually one or two kinds of target, that is, one or two flight lines (the paths the targets fly), which you shoot again and again. For example, today a crosser from left to right, which flies across in front of you, and an incomer, which flies towards you. You shoot each of them many times. Meanwhile the coach corrects your stance, your hold point (where the barrels wait as you call) and the way you move the gun from that point onto the target. Deep work on one kind of target often teaches a beginner more than one shot at each of twenty different targets. Once a target goes well, the next step is to mix it with others, as in a competition.

Doubles come after singles. First break each target of the pair on its own as a single. Then shoot them together: you already know where you will break each target, so you do not have to search for the second one.
If you are preparing for a competition, you can add a short task under mild pressure near the end, for example five targets in a row. How to build this up step by step: Training for competition.
Finish on targets that are already going well. You then leave with the picture of a good shot rather than your last miss. Confidence is part of technique too, as coaches often say.

After the session take a few minutes, alone or with your coach: what worked, what did not, what to work on next time. Write it in your training diary; how to keep one is explained in Training diary and measuring progress.

notes.html: Agree on one or two aims at the start of the session and check them together at the end. One short tip after a target often works better than a long explanation.

key_points.html: Warm-up: light movement and a few easy targets
Main part: one or two kinds of target, many repetitions
Doubles only after each target is broken on its own
Finish with targets that are going well
After the session: a short review and a note in your diary

did_you_know.html: Many coaches ask the shooter to name the break point, the place where they plan to break the target, before calling: the plan becomes clearer.

quiz.q: How many kinds of target does a beginner usually work on in the main part of a session?

options.text: All the targets the ground has
One or two, shot many times

quiz.explain: Many coaches find that deep work on one or two kinds of target brings a beginner more progress than single shots at many. Mixing targets comes later, once they go well.

quiz.q: How do many coaches suggest approaching a double?

options.text: Break each target alone first, then both together
Shoot both targets together from the start
Practise only the second target of the pair

quiz.explain: Then you already know where you will break each target of the double.

quiz.q: Which targets do many coaches suggest for the end of a session?

options.text: The hardest target of the day
Targets that are already going well
A long series until you are tired

quiz.explain: Ending on success builds confidence for the next session.
